children: Tata Sons can challenge the Reserve Bank of India’s rejection of its application to surrender its core investment company registration, though overturning the banking regulator’s decision could prove difficult given the limited scope of judicial review in economic and regulatory policy cases.
The RBI rejected Tata Sons’ deregistration application on September 11, bringing the holding company of the Tata Group closer to a stock market listing.
Tata Sons has been classified as an upper-layer non-banking financial company (NBFC-UL), a category that mandates listing within three years of being identified.
Legal options
The company’s most practical legal option is to file a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the Bombay High Court, challenging the RBI’s decision.
Article 32 offers a second route but Tata Sons would have establish a violation of a fundamental right to file its petition in the Supreme Court.

Tata Sons could argue that the RBI failed to adequately consider the fundamental change in its financial profile after it repaid its borrowings and became debt-free. It could also contend that the regulator applied the rules mechanically despite Tata Sons having no customer-facing lending business and being substantially owned by public charitable trusts.
The RBI’s framework is based not merely on outstanding borrowings but also on an entity’s size, activities and direct or indirect access to public funds.

The central bank said in April that funds received through associates or group entities having access to public funds would count as an indirect receipt of public funds. Several Tata Group companies that have invested in the holding company are themselves listed entities or have access to public debt markets.

A legal challenge could instead focus on whether the RBI gave Tata Sons sufficient reasons for rejecting the application, considered all relevant material and applied the same regulatory standards consistently.
The company may also question whether its activities satisfy the statutory definition of an NBFC or CIC after the restructuring of its balance sheet.
Emails sent to Tata Sons and Tata Trusts had not elicited a response at the time of publication of this article.
The RBI’s treatment of Shanghvi Finance, another industrial-group holding company included in the central bank’s first NBFC-Upper Layer list in 2022, could also be an argument for Tata Sons.

After repaying its debt, Shanghvi Finance surrendered its registration in February 2023, which the RBI cancelled with effect from May that year. Sanghvi Finance is a promoter group holding company of Sun Pharma.
Uday Kotak precedent
If it decides to use legal remedies, Tata Sons would not be the first major Indian corporate house to challenge the RBI in court.
In December 2018, Kotak Mahindra Bank moved the Bombay High Court against the regulator’s directions requiring promoter Uday Kotak to reduce his shareholding in the bank.
The lender argued that its issuance of non-convertible perpetual preference shares had brought the promoter’s holding within the prescribed regulatory ceiling, a position the RBI disputed.

The case did not produce a final ruling on merits. Kotak Mahindra Bank and the RBI reached a settlement in January 2020 under which Uday Kotak was allowed to retain a 26 percent economic stake, while his voting rights were capped at 15 percent. The bank subsequently withdrew its writ petition.
The episode shows that an RBI decision can be challenged and that litigation may create room for a negotiated regulatory solution.
However, unless the RBI reconsiders its position or a court intervenes, Tata Sons will continue to be governed as an upper-layer NBFC and remain subject to the accompanying listing requirements.

title: Can Tata Sons challenge RBI’s deregistration rejection?
